title: Writing Dockerfiles
description: Learn to write Dockerfiles with common instructions, best practices, and multi-stage builds.

data.text: A **Dockerfile** is a plain-text file containing a set of instructions that Docker Engine uses to automatically build an image. Each instruction corresponds to a line in the file and creates a new layer in the resulting image.

terms.definition: Sets the base image for the next instructions. This should be the first instruction in a Dockerfile.
Executes a command during the build, creating a new layer. Used for installing packages and compiling code.
Copies files from a source on the host to the filesystem of the image.
Sets the working directory inside the container. Equivalent to `cd` in a shell.
Provides default commands that run when a container starts. It can be overridden.
Configures a container to run as an executable. Unlike CMD, it is not easily overridable.

rows: Execute a command at build time
Document which port the app listens on
Default command to run at startup

data.title: Dockerfile for a Node.js app
data.content: This Dockerfile builds a container image for a Node.js application. It starts with an official base image, copies the dependencies file, installs packages, then copies the rest of the app.
data.code:
FROM node:20-alpine

WORKDIR /app

COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production

COPY . .

EXPOSE 3000

CMD ["node", "server.js"]

data.text: Notice the order: `COPY package*.json` comes before `COPY . .`. This means if only application code changes (but dependencies stay the same), Docker can use the cached layer of installed packages and skip reinstallation. This is a critical best practice.

For compiled languages like TypeScript, Go, or C#, you often need a build tool installed during image creation but not at runtime. **Multi-stage builds** let you use multiple `FROM` statements in a single Dockerfile. Each stage can copy artifacts from a previous stage, keeping the final image small.

data.title: Multi-stage build for a TypeScript app
data.content: The first stage installs dependencies and builds the TypeScript code. The second stage copies only the compiled output, leaving behind all build tools.
data.code:
FROM node:20-alpine AS builder

WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm install
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM node:20-alpine AS runtime

WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /app/dist ./dist
COPY --from=builder /app/package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production

EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "dist/index.js"]

data.caption: A Dockerfile builds an image in layers, from base image to final runtime.

cards.title: COPY
cards.description: Copies files and directories from the host into the image filesystem.

cards.title: ADD
cards.description: Like COPY, but also supports URL fetching and automatic tar extraction.

items: Use specific version tags instead of `latest` (e.g., `node:20-alpine`, not `node`).
Combine multiple `RUN` commands with `&&` to reduce image layers.
Put frequently changing operations last to maximize layer cache hits.
Use `.dockerignore` to exclude unnecessary files from the build context.
Prefer `COPY` over `ADD` unless you specifically need URL fetching or auto-extraction.
Always run containers as a non-root user with `USER`.

data.title: .dockerignore file
data.content: Exclude files that should never be sent to the Docker daemon during builds.

data.title: Avoid the `latest` trap
data.text: Using `latest` makes your builds non-reproducible. If the base image changes, your build may silently break. Always pin to a specific version.

data.title: Build your own image
data.description: Create a simple application container and run it locally.

Write a Dockerfile for your app.
Verify it works by opening http://localhost:8080 in a browser.
data.expectedOutcome: A running container serving your app on the host port you specified.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: A Dockerfile is a recipe for building a Docker image using layered instructions.
Instruction order matters: put rarely-changing steps first to benefit from cache.
Multi-stage builds keep final images small by discarding build-time dependencies.
Use `.dockerignore` and specific base image tags for reproducible, lean builds.
data.takeaway: A well-written Dockerfile is the foundation of reliable, reproducible container images.
